documents: Hosono, Takemura, Asahina & Otsubo 2022, Earth Planets Space 74:141, published PDF (13 pp.)

entry.evidence: However, the fluid flow behavior around the fault damage zone, including where it is supplied and released, remains to be established.

steps.action: Pose the open question of where fluids are supplied and released around a seismogenic thrust damage zone. Argue that core tests (too shallow) and wave-velocity estimates (low resolution) cannot resolve permeability structure at seismogenic depth.
steps.quote: the fluid flow behavior around the fault damage zone, including where it is supplied and released, remains to be established.

steps.action: Take up Oda's permeability tensor theory and its earlier two-dimensional applications to mineral-filled cracks (Ioannou and Spooner; FracPaQ software) as the starting tool.
steps.quote: Ioannou and Spooner (12) applied Oda’s permeability tensor in two dimensions to thermal cracks filled with mineral

steps.action: Choose the exhumed Nobeoka Thrust outcrop as an onshore analog of the Nankai seismogenic megathrust, where past fluid pathways are preserved as quartz veins.
steps.quote: This location is considered to be an onshore analog of the seismogenic fault of the Nankai Trough megathrust earthquake

steps.action: Build a three-dimensional procedure for Oda's tensor: veins as parallel-plate disks under the cubic law; P_ij rewritten via statistical independence and stereology (S0 from scanline intersections) so that aperture, orientation and m(q) from the outcrop suffice; four auxiliary assumptions stated; result read as first-order magnitude.
steps.quote: When estimating the paleo-permeability, the following assumptions are made in this study with reference to those of Ioannou and Spooner (12).

steps.action: Design two premise checks: a one-tailed chi-square test of independence among dip direction, length and aperture at 5%, and a convergence test of S0 with scanning-line length to satisfy the representative elementary volume.
steps.quote: The Chi-square test is a one-tailed test calculated at a significance level of 5%.

steps.action: Adopt the published stress inversion showing that the tensile crack-filling veins opened by slip of the Nobeoka Thrust during earthquakes, plus the published geology and displacement estimates.
steps.quote: The stress inversion of the tensile crack-filling vein shows that these fractures were opened by the slip of the Nobeoka Thrust during the earthquake

steps.action: Measure dip direction, dip angle, aperture (crack-width ruler, 0.05 mm limit) and length of quartz veins in the field. Exclude veins shorter than 30 mm, veins with slickenlines and veins crossing a whole grid; split bent veins in two; take thin sections.
steps.quote: the veins with slicken lines on the surface that preserve the shear movement were excluded.

steps.action: Lay out seven footwall grids (A to G) east to west across the fault, with a 2.5 m side set from the rule of at least 10 times the average vein length. Pick sites free of uneven ground and above high tide.
steps.quote: Therefore, the length of one side of the grid was set as 2.5 m to fully satisfy this condition.

steps.action: Draw vein trace maps on grid photographs, digitize vein endpoints, and count intersections m(q) on north-south and east-west scanning lines to obtain S0.
steps.quote: the coordinates of the endpoints of the quartz veins on the base trace map were determined using a digitizer.

steps.action: Check under the microscope (thin sections) that the measured veins record a single opening event, as the single-event premise requires. Note that other veins show repeated sealing.
steps.quote: Therefore, the quartz veins were used for measurement in this study because they were most likely formed during a single event.

steps.action: Plot vein poles on stereonets per grid and identify unimodal and bimodal orientation sets that change from grid to grid.
steps.quote: Grids A, B–D, and E–G exhibit E–W, NNE–SSW, and N–S quartz vein orientations, respectively.

steps.action: Run the chi-square tests on orientation, length and aperture and declare them independent. Vary total scanning-line length from 2.5 to 40 m and fix 30 m, where the relative error of S0 is within 20%.
steps.quote: These results indicate that the direction, length, direction, and aperture were statistically independent of each other.

steps.action: Compute the paleo-permeability tensor k_ij and its principal values for each grid (k1 2.99e-10 to 1.31e-9 m2, k3 1.16e-10 to 6.99e-10 m2).
steps.quote: The estimated paleo-permeability and related parameters are shown in Table 1 and Fig. 9.

steps.action: Compare the estimates with Nankai core-scale laboratory permeabilities (10^-20 to 10^-15 m2) and with earlier field-scale vein-based paleo-permeabilities; explain the differences by scale and by the isotropic averaging used elsewhere.
steps.quote: These permeabilities were measured from core size specimens and were smaller than the permeability at the field scale.

steps.action: Interpret the principal directions: k1 is roughly perpendicular to the fault plane, pointing to fluid migration toward the fault or hanging wall. Classify the grids into three anisotropy types linked to vein-orientation variability.
steps.quote: suggests that the fluid migrated more readily toward the fault plane or hanging wall.

steps.action: Explain Grid A's lower-than-expected permeability, despite its longer and thicker veins, by a possible underestimate of S0 caused by near-horizontal veins, rather than revising the estimate.
steps.quote: This may be because the veins in Grid A had more horizontally oriented veins than other Grids

steps.action: Compare the distance-from-core trend (highest paleo-permeability in Grid A, nearest the core) with published increases in damage-zone permeability toward the fault core.
steps.quote: Our results correspond with those of Lockner et al. (19), who noted that permeability was particularly high in the damage zone

steps.action: Keep the three-dimensional estimates of the maximum, intermediate and minimum paleo-permeabilities and their flow directions.
steps.quote: We estimated the maximum, intermediate, and minimum permeabilities and the associated direction of flow in three dimensions.

steps.action: Keep the method as viable for three-dimensional permeability estimation, deferring checks on anisotropic veins and on the density-connectivity relation to future numerical work.
steps.quote: Therefore, the proposed method, which analyzes observable geometric information, is a viable approach for three-dimensional permeability estimation.

steps.action: Set the inferred footwall-to-fault flow direction against the fault-valve model and declare it consistent.
steps.quote: This result is consistent with the fault-valve model

tree.answer: Past fluid migration in a thrust damage zone, recorded by tensile quartz veins
No; paleo-permeability is latent and is inferred from vein geometry through Oda's tensor
Estimate a 3D paleo-permeability tensor and develop the field method to do so
No rival hypotheses stated; fault-valve model is background only
Conditions found: exhumed outcrop traces at seven footwall grids
Premise checks only: chi-square independence, scanline convergence, thin-section single-event check
Estimate kept at first-order magnitude with ~20% S0 error
No review file supplied; reviewers are only thanked

end.claim: From quartz-vein geometry, the 3D paleo-permeability tensor in the Nobeoka Thrust footwall damage zone has principal values of about 10^-10 to 10^-9 m2 (S0-related error within ~20%, interpreted to first order of magnitude). Maximum paleo-permeability is highest near the fault core and oriented roughly perpendicular to the fault plane.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the stereology-based reformulation of Oda's tensor, which yields a 3D P_ij from outcrop aperture, orientation and scanline counts, no 3D paleo-permeability estimate would exist.

gates.evidence: No stated hypothesis directed the field acquisition; the grids sample distance from the fault and the fault-valve model is invoked only afterwards (§4 ¶1). The premises faced tests that could fail: chi-square independence (§3.2 ¶1) and S0 convergence (§3.2 ¶2). The permeability estimate itself is not tested against any independent measurement, and the fault-valve comparison is a consistency statement. The 5% significance level, the 10x-length grid rule and the 2.5 m grid size were fixed in advance, the grid size from a prior survey of vein lengths (§2.3 ¶1, §2.4 ¶3). The 30 m scanline length was chosen after the convergence data were seen.

imports.item: Oda's permeability tensor and crack/fabric tensor theory, used at excavations, dams and geothermal sites
Cubic law for laminar parallel-plate flow and Darcy's law
Stereological estimate of fracture surface density S0 from scanline intersections
Representative volume element convergence criterion (Kanit et al. 2003)
Crack width ruler for aperture measurement

novelty_claims.quote: we have not only applied Oda’s permeability tensor theory to estimate three-dimensional paleo-permeability in the damage zone around a thrust fault
[...] also developed in situ analytic methods to estimate a three-dimensional paleo-permeability tensor
which renders high-resolution permeability structure in the seismogenic zone

limits: Sub-claims: the method is capability_characterized only through premise checks (§4 ¶1), not by comparison with any measured permeability. The fluid-migration direction and its consistency with the fault-valve model is an interpretation with no stated rival, so no confirmed or best_explanation status can be given (§3.4 ¶1, §4 ¶1). The distance-from-core trend is a qualitative agreement with Lockner et al. (2009). Not shown about the process: (1) The chi-square logic reads inverted. All p-values fall below 5% and 'the statistical hypothesis was rejected', yet the authors conclude independence (§3.2 ¶1); which null was tested is not stated (inference). (2) The text contradicts itself on Grid A: 'low permeability' in §3.4 ¶1 against the highest footwall paleo-permeability in §3.4 ¶2. (3) Fig. 4c,d shows multiple-sealing veins, but how such veins were excluded from the grid data is not stated. (4) The ~20% error covers only S0 convergence. The auxiliaries (impermeable host, full connectivity with lambda=1, aperture unchanged by precipitation, cubic law) are assumed, not varied. (5) No independent permeability data, no replication on another fault, no hanging-wall grids. Data availability is 'Not applicable'. (6) A review occurred (acknowledgements) but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Composition none_fits: the walk is a method extension applied to a trace record with no rivals and no repeated phenomenon. capability_first is closest, but here the question precedes the capability.

disagreements.target: Previous 2D applications of Oda's tensor (FracPaQ, Healy et al. 2017; Ioannou and Spooner 2007)
disagreements.support: The authors extend the tensor to three dimensions with stereology and in situ data; there is no quantitative comparison with the 2D results.
disagreements.quote: they were limited to estimating two-dimensional permeability tensor

disagreements.target: Laboratory core permeability and wave-velocity permeability estimates (Kato et al. 2004; Nakajima and Uchida 2018)
disagreements.support: An argument from depth coverage and resolution only.
disagreements.quote: [...] provided permeability in a shallower area than the seismogenic zone, and the latter provided a low-resolution permeability structure

disagreements.target: Nankai drill-core laboratory permeabilities (Ikari et al. 2009; Tanikawa et al. 2012, 2014)
disagreements.support: The field-scale estimates are several orders of magnitude higher, which the authors attribute to the absence of wide, long open fractures in core-size specimens.
disagreements.quote: [...] wider and longer open fractures are not reflected in core size permeability.

disagreements.target: Gilbert et al. (2018) vein-based isotropic permeability
disagreements.support: The authors argue that an isotropic average k_ii/3 underestimates the maximum principal permeability, so a tensor is needed when anisotropy matters.
disagreements.quote: Gilbert et al. (6) estimated the permeability from the width and density of mineral veins and did not separate them by direction.

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Laboratory testing of core specimens; estimation from wave velocity
alternatives_considered.reason: Cores sample shallower than the seismogenic zone; wave velocity gives low resolution

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Cubic law modified by a roughness or contact-area coefficient (Witherspoon et al.; Zimmerman et al.)
alternatives_considered.reason: Veins are smooth tensile cracks with no contact area formed under high water pressure

alternatives_considered.chosen: Straight tensile veins longer than 30 mm without slickenlines and not crossing a whole grid; bent veins split in two
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Including shear veins with slickenlines and grid-crossing veins longer than 10 m
alternatives_considered.reason: Tensile veins are taken to record a single seismic event; strike and dip are accurate only above 30 mm
S0 converges from ~20 m, and 30 m keeps the relative error within 0.2

alternatives_considered.chosen: Full permeability tensor with principal values
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Isotropic average k_ii/3, as in Gilbert et al. (2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: Anisotropy matters; the average underestimates k1
